youtube.title: Variables and Types in C++: int, double, char, bool | C++ Programming EP 05
youtube.description: In this episode you will create variables of type int, double, char and bool, pick the right type for a value and give every variable a starting value, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:16 Variables and types · 1:37 Four variables · 2:56 Variables in memory · 3:47 Second program · 5:10 Recap · 5:42 Bug of the Day · 6:47 Challenge · 7:14 Next episode

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Until now, our programs only printed words. Today they learn to remember things. You will make boxes for numbers, letters and yes or no answers.

scenes.onScreen: "Variables and types": numbered lines (1. A variable is a named box in memory; 2. Every box has a type; 3. The type says what can go inside) and an analogy card: a beach shack fridge: one shelf for bottles, one tray for ice
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A variable is a named box in memory. Every box has a type, and the type says what can go inside. Int holds whole numbers, like three fish. Double holds numbers with a decimal point. Char holds one single character. Bool holds only true or false. Think of a beach shack fridge. One shelf is for bottles, and one tray is for ice. Each place fits one job. Why does C plus plus ask for a type at all? The type tells the compiler how much room the box needs. It also tells the compiler what the bits inside mean. The same bits can be a number or a letter, so the type decides. A good name helps as much as a good type. Write fish count, not x. When you read the code next month, the name tells you the story.
points: A variable is a named box in memory
The type says what can go inside

scenes.onScreen: vars.cpp: four variables, each line shows type, name and value
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 5] Int fish equals three. First comes the type, then the name, then the value. [HL 6] Double price equals one hundred twenty point five. [HL 7] Char grade equals A. Notice the single quotes around the letter. [HL 8] Bool open now equals true. [HL 9] Now we print each one. The names have no quotes, so cout prints the value inside the box, not the name. [HL 5] Read this line from left to right. The type is int, the name is fish, and the value is three. The equals sign here puts the value into the box. [HL 7] A char holds exactly one letter, so we use single quotes. Double quotes are for whole words, and they mean a different type. [HL 8] Bool prints as one for true and zero for false, unless you ask for words. [HL 12] So the last line prints the number one on your screen.

scenes.onScreen: four memory boxes with value, size in bytes and address
scenes.animation: Boxes pop in one by one with size and address tags; arrows draw on as the narrator mentions them; regions are labelled; pop per box
scenes.narration: Here is what memory looks like. Each variable is a box with a name, a value and an address. An int takes four bytes on most computers. A double is bigger. It takes eight bytes. A char takes one byte, and so does a bool. Different types have different sizes. Notice that two variables never share a box. Each name has its own address. The address is where the box starts in memory. The computer reads exactly as many bytes as the type needs, and then it stops.

scenes.onScreen: sizes.cpp: sizeof shows how many bytes each type uses
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 5] The sizeof operator tells us how many bytes a type needs. [HL 5] For int, it prints four. [HL 6] A double needs eight bytes. [HL 7] A char needs one byte. [HL 8] A bool needs one byte as well. These numbers match the boxes we saw before. [HL 5] The sizeof operator does not run any code at all. The compiler works out the answer while it builds the program. The numbers four and eight are common, but the language does not promise them for every computer. Use sizeof when you need to be sure on your own machine.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as sizes dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. Each line shows the size of one type. The numbers are four, eight, one and one. Your numbers may differ on another computer, but these four are normal on a modern laptop.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A variable is a named box with a type. Two. Use int for whole numbers and double for decimals. Three. Use char for one letter and bool for true or false. Four. Always give a variable a starting value. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: A variable is a named box with a type.
Use int for whole numbers and double for decimals.
Use char for one letter and bool for true or false.
Always give a variable a starting value.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A variable with no starting value
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the g++ warning appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the warning goes away with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. Here we make an int called packets, but we never give it a value. The compiler warns us that packets is used uninitialized. The program still builds, but it prints a strange number. That number is garbage left in memory. Give every variable a value when you make it. Garbage values are tricky, because the program may print zero on one run and a strange number on the next. That makes the bug hard to catch. So make it a habit. Whenever you write a variable, write its first value in the same line.

scenes.onScreen: An uninitialised variable walks into a bar. The bartender asks, what will you have? It says, whatever was there before.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw

scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Make four variables: your age, your height in metres, your first initial and whether you like fish. Print all four. Hint: pick one type for each value. A height has decimals, so it is a double. Write your answer in the comments.

bug.error:
Compiler output (a warning, the program still builds):

packets.cpp: In function 'int main()':
packets.cpp:6:28: warning: 'packets' is used uninitialized [-Wuninitialized]
    6 |     cout << "Packets: " << packets << endl;
      |                            ^~~~~~~
packets.cpp:5:9: note: 'packets' was declared here
    5 |     int packets;
bug.why: A variable that you do not set holds whatever was in that memory before. Always write a starting value, such as zero.

challengeAnswer: Use int, double, char and bool. For example, use seventeen, one point six five, the letter A and true. The bool prints as one.
